title: “I HAVE DONE NO WRONG.” — THE TERRIFYING WORDS OF A WOMAN WHO COMMITTED ADULTERY
paragraphs: “I HAVE DONE NO WRONG.” — THE TERRIFYING WORDS OF A WOMAN WHO COMMITTED ADULTERY

Proverbs 30:20 exposes something more frightening than the act of adultery itself: a heart that has learned to sin, erase the evidence, silence its conscience, and walk away believing it has nothing to confess. But what happens when Jesus confronts the sins we have become experts at hiding?
There is a kind of sinner who cries after falling.
And there is a kind of sinner who no longer feels the fall.
One trembles because the conscience is still awake. The other sleeps peacefully because the conscience has learned to stop asking questions.
One whispers, “God, what have I done?”
The other looks at the wreckage, straightens their clothes, returns to ordinary life, and says something that should make every human soul tremble.
“I have done no wrong.”
Five words.
No tears. No confession. No trembling. No visible remorse.
And perhaps the most disturbing part is that the person saying them may genuinely believe them.
Imagine a woman returning home after betraying her marriage vows.
She knows where she has been. She knows what happened. She knows what she promised before God. She knows the trust she has violated.
Yet the next morning, she can sit at the same table, exchange familiar words, carry on with ordinary responsibilities, and behave as though nothing has happened.
Her outward composure tells you nothing about whether her conscience is troubled.
Perhaps she has convinced herself that her circumstances justified her actions.
Perhaps she has repeated her excuses so many times that they now sound like truth.
Perhaps she has simply decided that something is only wrong when someone discovers it.

Scripture does not tell us her biography, her husband's response, or what happens afterward. But it gives us a picture so brief and penetrating that thousands of years later it still reaches into the hidden chambers of the human heart.
“Such is the way of an adulterous woman; she eateth, and wipeth her mouth, and saith, I have done no wickedness.” — Proverbs 30:20, KJV
Read that again.
She eats.
She wipes her mouth.
She says she has done nothing wrong.
The writer does not describe a dramatic escape, a courtroom confrontation, or an elaborate conspiracy.
He describes something ordinary.
Eating. Wiping. Speaking.
And that is precisely what makes the image so unsettling.
The sin is treated as casually as finishing a meal.
No visible disruption. No outward acknowledgment. Nothing that suggests the gravity of what has happened.
The Hebrew makes the picture even sharper.
The opening words are:
כֵּן דֶּרֶךְ אִשָּׁה מְנָאָפֶת
Ken derekh ishah mena'afet.
Literally, “Thus is the way of an adulterous woman.”
The word דֶּרֶךְ (derekh) means “way,” “road,” or “path.” In biblical wisdom literature, it frequently describes a person's manner of life or pattern of conduct.
This is not merely a statement about one isolated moment. It presents a recognizable way of behaving.
Then comes the chilling sequence:
אָכְלָה וּמָחֲתָה פִיהָ
Akhlah u-machatah piha.
“She eats and wipes her mouth.”
The language is deliberately ordinary. The eating and wiping form a vivid comparison for treating wrongdoing as something easily completed and dismissed.
And then the final declaration:
וְאָמְרָה לֹא־פָעַלְתִּי אָוֶן
Ve'amrah, lo-fa'alti aven.
“And she says, ‘I have done no wrong.’”
The Hebrew word אָוֶן (aven) can refer to wickedness, wrongdoing, or iniquity.
She does not merely say, “Nobody caught me.”
She declares that she has committed no wrongdoing.
The proverb exposes the horrifying possibility of moral denial.
A person can do something objectively wrong and still insist on innocence.
A person can become so practiced at rationalizing sin that confession begins to feel unnecessary.
But there is something important we must understand before we turn this verse into a weapon against someone else.
Proverbs 30:20 is not permission to stereotype women or to suggest that adultery belongs to one gender.
It describes an adulterous woman, but Scripture condemns sexual unfaithfulness in both men and women.
Jesus goes even deeper, exposing the lust that can already corrupt the heart before an outward act occurs (Matthew 5:27–28).
The woman in the proverb is not an invitation to point fingers at every woman who has fallen.
She is a mirror held before every person who has ever found a way to excuse what God calls sin.
And if we are courageous enough to look into that mirror, we may discover something we did not expect.
The most dangerous words in the passage might not be the words of an adulterous woman.
They might be words we have spoken ourselves.
Not necessarily about adultery.
About the lie we called self-protection.
The bitterness we called discernment.
The cruelty we called honesty.
The gossip we called concern.
The pride we called confidence.
The dishonesty we called survival.
The lust we called harmless entertainment.
The secret relationship we called emotional support.
The unforgiveness we called boundaries, even when our true desire was revenge.
Not every boundary is unforgiveness. Not every painful relationship is sinful. Not every struggle is rebellion.
But sometimes we borrow respectable words to protect things we do not want God to confront.
And the frightening question is not merely whether we have sinned.
It is whether we have become comfortable explaining away the very thing that is destroying us.
You can convince your friends.
You can manipulate appearances.
You can delete conversations.
You can erase browsing history.
You can change passwords.
You can construct an entire version of your life that makes you look innocent.
But there is one place where no deleted message, rehearsed explanation, or polished reputation can conceal the truth.
Before God.
Hebrews 4:13 says:
“Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do.” (KJV)
That verse should sober us.
But it should also awaken hope.
Because the God who sees everything is also the God who invites sinners to come into the light.
And that is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Think about the last time your conscience troubled you.
Maybe it happened in the middle of a conversation.
You said something cruel, and immediately felt the weight of it.
But instead of apologizing, you replayed everything the other person had done to provoke you.
By the time you finished rehearsing their failures, your own words no longer seemed so terrible.
Or perhaps you crossed a boundary in a relationship.
At first, you knew something was wrong.
The messages became more intimate.
The conversations became more secretive.
You started sharing parts of your heart with someone you knew you should not be pursuing.
You told yourself it was innocent.
Then you began hiding it.
And when the hiding itself should have warned you, you found another explanation.
“They understand me.”
“My spouse doesn't listen.”
“Nothing physical has happened.”
“I deserve to be happy.”
Those statements may contain genuine pain. Some relationships do involve neglect, mistreatment, or deep loneliness. Such suffering deserves compassionate attention and appropriate help.
But pain does not automatically make every response righteous.
Being wounded does not give us permission to wound others.
And loneliness, however real, does not transform betrayal into faithfulness.
This is why Proverbs 30:20 is so disturbing.
It does not merely reveal the existence of sin.
It reveals how a person may become skilled at living beside sin without acknowledging it.
The longer we justify something, the easier it can become to stop questioning it.
The longer we hide something, the more normal hiding can begin to feel.
And eventually, a person may mistake the absence of immediate consequences for the approval of God.
But silence is not approval.
Delay is not innocence.
And a conscience that no longer protests is not necessarily a conscience that has become holy.

The apostle Paul speaks of people whose consciences have been seared (1 Timothy 4:2). That passage addresses false teaching and hypocrisy, but it illustrates the biblical seriousness of a conscience damaged by persistent falsehood.
Sin is not harmless merely because it has become familiar.
And a person is not spiritually safe merely because they no longer feel guilty.
Yet here is a distinction we desperately need.
Feeling guilty does not automatically mean you are guilty, and feeling innocent does not automatically mean you are right.
Our feelings must be examined in the light of God's Word.
Some tenderhearted believers carry crushing shame over things for which they have already repented and received forgiveness.
Others experience genuine conviction and immediately attempt to silence it.
The answer for neither person is to make feelings the final judge.
The answer is truth.
God's truth.
And God's truth does not merely expose.
It also offers a way home.
Consider the setting of this proverb.
Proverbs 30:18–19 describes four things that amaze Agur: the way of an eagle in the sky, a serpent on a rock, a ship on the sea, and a man with a young woman.
Then verse 20 presents the way of an adulterous woman who eats, wipes her mouth, and denies wrongdoing.
The surrounding imagery involves ways or paths that are mysterious, difficult to trace, or astonishing to observe.
The final verse introduces a disturbing moral contrast: someone can commit wrongdoing and then behave as though nothing happened.

We should be careful not to claim that the proverb explicitly teaches every detail of a secret affair or that its primary point is the psychology of every adulterer. Its image is concise, and its literary setting matters.
But its moral warning is unmistakable.
Wrongdoing can be followed by brazen denial.
And the human heart is capable of astonishing self-deception.
Now imagine that same heart encountering Jesus.
Not the comfortable Jesus we sometimes invent to approve everything we already want.
Not a religious symbol used to decorate a life we refuse to surrender.
The Jesus revealed in Scripture.
Holy.
Merciful.
Truthful.
Compassionate.
Unwilling to call darkness light.
Unwilling to abandon sinners who come to Him in repentance.
In John 4, Jesus meets a Samaritan woman at a well.
She arrives seeking water.
She leaves having encountered someone who knows the truth about her life.
Jesus tells her that she has had five husbands and that the man she currently has is not her husband (John 4:17–18).
Scripture does not tell us the circumstances of her previous marriages, so we must not assume that every relationship ended because of her wrongdoing.
But Jesus knows her history.
He does not need gossip.
He does not need an investigation.
He does not need someone to expose her.
He already knows.
And still He speaks with her.
Still He offers living water.
Still He reveals Himself to her.
The encounter does not end with her being discarded as a hopeless case.
It leads to testimony.
The woman goes into the city and says:
“Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?” (John 4:29, KJV)
Notice the astonishing reversal.
She does not build her testimony around the idea that Jesus knows nothing about her past.
She tells people that He knows.
The very knowledge that could have terrified her becomes part of her invitation for others to encounter Him.
And many Samaritans believe because of her testimony, as John 4:39 records.
What a picture of grace.
Jesus does not need your past to remain hidden before He can begin transforming your future.
He already knows.
And He still calls you to come.
But the Gospel never tells us that grace means pretending sin is harmless.
Consider another encounter.
In John 8:3–11, the scribes and Pharisees bring a woman caught in adultery before Jesus.
They place her in the middle of a public confrontation.

The passage itself has a significant textual-history issue: the account is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John and appears in different locations in parts of the manuscript tradition. It has nevertheless been treasured and received in much of Christian tradition. We should acknowledge that textual question rather than conceal it.
Within the familiar account, Jesus refuses to join the accusers' trap.
He confronts their readiness to condemn.
And when the accusers have gone, He says to the woman:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11, KJV)
Two truths stand together.
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin.
Jesus does not say adultery was acceptable.
He does not say repentance is unnecessary.
But neither does He treat the woman as beyond the reach of mercy.
And this is the Gospel we desperately need to recover.
Not a message that makes sin seem small.
Not a message that makes forgiveness seem impossible.
A Savior who tells the truth about both.
Because if we minimize sin, we will never understand the depth of grace.
And if we minimize grace, we will never understand the hope available to sinners.
Perhaps that is why the most frightening person in Proverbs 30:20 is not necessarily the person with the worst public reputation.
It is the person who sees no reason to repent.
Jesus once told a parable about two men praying in the temple.
One was a Pharisee.
The other was a tax collector.
The Pharisee thanked God that he was not like other sinners.
He recited his religious achievements.
He appeared confident in his righteousness.
The tax collector stood at a distance.
He would not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
Instead, he prayed:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.” (Luke 18:13, KJV)
Jesus said the tax collector went home justified rather than the other man.
Why?
Not because sin was unimportant.
Not because repentance earned God's favor.
But because the tax collector abandoned his claim to self-righteousness and appealed to God's mercy.
The Pharisee had religious language.
The tax collector had a broken plea.
The Pharisee compared himself with other people.
The tax collector recognized his own need.
And the parable asks every religious reader an uncomfortable question.
What if the greatest obstacle between you and repentance is your insistence that you have nothing to repent of?
You can attend church every Sunday and still be hiding something.
You can memorize Bible verses and still refuse correction.
You can lead worship and still mistreat your family.
You can publish Christian messages and still secretly nourish pride.
You can teach others about holiness while resisting the very truth you proclaim.
That includes those of us who write, preach, teach, and serve in ministry.
A platform is not proof of purity.
A large audience is not evidence that God approves of everything happening behind the scenes.
A religious reputation cannot substitute for a surrendered heart.
And this is not a call to live in constant terror, obsessively searching for sins that may not exist.
It is a call to humble, honest examination before the Lord.
Psalm 139:23–24 gives us words to pray:
“Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.” (KJV)
Notice what the psalmist does not pray.
“Lord, help me prove I am innocent.”
He invites God to search him.
He is willing to be corrected.
He wants to be led.
And perhaps that is the prayer some of us have been avoiding.
Because we know that if we sincerely ask God to search our hearts, we may have to face things we have carefully protected.
A relationship we need to end.
A lie we need to correct.
Money we need to return.
An apology we need to make.
A pattern of manipulation we need to confess.
A private habit we need to confront.
A wound for which we need wise help rather than another excuse.
Repentance may involve painful consequences.
Trust may need to be rebuilt slowly.
Some relationships may never return to what they were.
Forgiveness does not mean that victims must abandon boundaries, remain in unsafe situations, or immediately restore access to someone who has harmed them.
And when wrongdoing includes abuse, coercion, or danger, seeking safety and appropriate support is not a failure of Christian forgiveness.
God's mercy does not require us to pretend that evil has caused no damage.
Real repentance takes truth seriously.
But it also takes the cross seriously.
Because Christianity does not proclaim that we save ourselves by becoming sufficiently ashamed.
It proclaims that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Listen to the apostle Paul:
“This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” (1 Timothy 1:15, KJV)
Paul knew what it meant to have a past.
He had persecuted the church.
He had participated in terrible wrongdoing while believing he was serving God.
He knew the danger of religious zeal without true understanding.
Yet the risen Christ confronted him.
And the persecutor became a witness to the grace of the One he had opposed.
Paul's story did not become beautiful because his past suddenly became harmless.
It became a testimony because Christ's mercy was greater than his former rebellion.
That is redemption.
Not the rewriting of history to make sin look innocent.
But the rewriting of a life through the grace and transforming power of Jesus Christ.
And this is where our theme becomes more than a memorable phrase.
Not because Jesus calls adultery faithfulness.
Not because He calls lies truth.
Not because He calls rebellion righteousness.
But because the Savior who died for our sins and rose again can forgive the repentant, reconcile us to God, and make us new.
The cross does not erase the moral seriousness of our choices.
It reveals how serious sin is and how astonishing God's love truly is.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had successfully hidden the evidence.
Not after we had manufactured a flawless reputation.
Not after we had convinced everyone that nothing was wrong.
Christ died for sinners.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and new life are offered to those who turn to Him in faith.
That is why 1 John 1:8–9 matters so much.
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
And then comes the promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Look at the contrast.
Proverbs 30:20 shows someone saying, “I have done no wrong.”
First John warns that claiming to be without sin is self-deception.
And then it shows the way forward.
Confession.
Not because God needs information.
He already knows.
Confession matters because we stop defending the lie and agree with the truth.
We stop calling darkness light.
We stop asking God to bless what He has commanded us to forsake.
We stop treating repentance as humiliation and begin seeing it as the doorway back into honest fellowship with Him.
The Greek word translated “confess” in 1 John 1:9 is ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen), from a verb commonly meaning “to acknowledge” or “confess.”
It carries the sense of openly acknowledging what is true.
Confession is not a performance designed to purchase forgiveness.
It is the honest acknowledgment of sin before the God who forgives through Christ.
And that is where the exhausted soul can finally stop pretending.
You do not have to convince Jesus that you are someone you are not.
You do not have to make your past sound prettier than it was.
You do not have to turn every mistake into someone else's fault.
You do not have to hide behind religious language.
You can tell Him the truth.
“Lord, I lied.”
“Lord, I betrayed someone's trust.”
“Lord, I have been proud.”
“Lord, I have been hiding.”
“Lord, I keep returning to something I know is wrong.”
“Lord, I need mercy.”
And if you are struggling to find the words, remember the tax collector's prayer.
“God be merciful to me a sinner.”
No elaborate speech.
No impressive vocabulary.
Just a sinner appealing to mercy.
Perhaps you are reading this with tears in your eyes.
Perhaps you have spent years carrying the consequences of a decision you deeply regret.
Perhaps you are the person who was betrayed.
You remember the discovery.
The shaking hands.
The questions.
The painful realization that someone you trusted had been living a different story behind your back.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
The wrongdoing committed against you was not made acceptable by the excuses used to defend it.
Your pain matters.
Your need for truth matters.
Your safety matters.
And you are not required to call betrayal harmless in order to honor Christ.
The Lord who calls sinners to repentance also cares about those wounded by sin.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.” (KJV)
Or perhaps you are the person who betrayed someone.
You are reading this because the description in Proverbs feels uncomfortably familiar.
You know what it is like to minimize.
To explain.
To hide.
To say, “It wasn't that serious.”
To say, “Everybody does it.”
To say, “No one got hurt.”
And deep down, you know those explanations have not made you free.
There is still a way forward.
Not through another lie.
Not through religious activity used as camouflage.
Not through a promise that you will simply try harder while keeping the same secrets.
Through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
Through bringing your life into the light.
Through accepting responsibility and seeking wise, appropriate accountability.
Through allowing the Holy Spirit to transform what you cannot heal by appearances alone.
Second Corinthians 7:10 speaks of godly sorrow that produces repentance leading to salvation, in contrast to worldly sorrow.
There is a difference between grieving because you were exposed and grieving because you have sinned.
There is a difference between wanting consequences to disappear and wanting your heart to change.
There is a difference between regretting that people found out and recognizing that you have offended a holy God and harmed others.
And yet even here, we must be careful.
We cannot perfectly measure another person's repentance by the number of tears they shed.
Some people weep easily.
Others struggle to express emotion.
The deeper question is whether there is genuine turning toward God, truth, and obedience.
Repentance is not merely an emotional moment.
It is a change of direction that bears fruit over time.
And transformation is possible because Jesus Christ is alive.
The same Lord who conquered death is not powerless before your habits, your pride, your shame, or your past.
That does not mean healing is always immediate.
It does not mean every relationship will be restored.
It does not mean consequences vanish.
But it means your story does not have to end in the place where sin left you.
Now, there is something else I want you to consider.
What if someone you love is living in the very kind of denial Proverbs describes?
What if they are not ready to listen to you?
What if every conversation becomes another argument?
You cannot force repentance into another person's heart.
You cannot become their Savior.
You cannot control whether they choose honesty.
But you can speak truth with love, refuse to participate in deception, maintain wise boundaries, pray, and entrust what you cannot control to God.
And you can examine your own heart without making another person's wrongdoing an excuse for yours.
Because this passage was never meant to turn us into self-appointed detectives obsessed with everyone else's hidden life.
It was meant to awaken reverence for God and honesty before Him.
So before you close this article, I want to ask you something.
Not for a public performance.
Not to pressure you into revealing a private sin.
Not to make you feel that a comment on social media is the same thing as repentance before God.
But because sometimes the first small act of honesty is admitting that we still need prayer.
If your spirit has been exhausted from fighting a battle no one else sees, you can comment, “Pray for me.”
You do not need to explain the details.
And if this Scripture has reminded you that Christ is still transforming your life, you can write, “Christ is still healing me.”
Let those words become an invitation for fellow believers to encourage one another, not a substitute for prayer, repentance, pastoral care, or practical change.
And please, do not read the comments merely to judge the people who respond.
Remember that every person who admits a struggle is someone in need of grace.
Just as we are.
Not as a weapon.
Not as a public accusation.
But as a reminder that the door of repentance is still open.
You never know who is reading silently at midnight.
A husband wrestling with temptation.
A wife carrying the pain of betrayal.
A young believer trying to break a destructive pattern.
A church leader afraid to confess a secret.
A person who has been away from Christ for years and wonders whether coming home is still possible.
And if someone comes to mind, consider tagging them only when doing so would genuinely encourage rather than embarrass them. A private message may sometimes be the more loving choice.
God's truth exposes what is wrong so that we may turn to the One who makes us new.

We want this to be a place where biblical truth is not watered down, where wounded people are treated with compassion, where repentance is preached without hypocrisy, and where the saving work of Jesus Christ remains at the center.
These resources are intended to help believers move beyond momentary inspiration into deeper understanding of Scripture, prayer, Christian maturity, and a more faithful walk with Jesus.
There are people who will never walk into the church you attend.
People who are too ashamed to ask a question publicly.
People who cannot afford a shelf full of Christian books.
People who are quietly searching for answers about Jesus on a phone screen.
If Gospel Warrior can place sound biblical teaching, free resources, and Christ-centered encouragement within their reach, that is work worth continuing.
But producing, maintaining, and expanding those resources takes real time, effort, and financial support.
For believers who wish to make it part of their regular Christian giving, it can be one expression of generosity.
Scripture teaches generous, willing giving, not giving extracted through guilt.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That is the spirit in which I invite you.
Not because you must pay to receive God's favor.
Not because grace has a monthly price.
But because voluntary generosity can help good work continue.
If you are already supporting your church, caring for your family, or navigating financial hardship, please honor those responsibilities wisely.
Those acts matter, too.
These are simply thank-you benefits for those who help sustain the work. They are not the reason we preach Christ, and they do not make anyone more spiritually deserving than another believer.
Keep reading His Word.
Keep praying.
Keep growing in a faithful local church.
Keep returning to the Gospel when your heart becomes weary.
Because our deepest hope is not to build an audience that depends on a ministry.
It is to help people know and follow the Savior.
And before we finish, I want to return to that woman in Proverbs.
She eats.
She wipes her mouth.
She says, “I have done no wrong.”
We are not told that she repented.
We are not told that she confessed.
We are not told that her heart changed.
The proverb leaves us staring at the terrible calmness of denial.
But you and I are not required to imitate her response.
We can choose another prayer.
We can say, “Lord, I have done wrong.”
We can stop defending what needs to be confessed.
We can stop hiding what needs to be brought into the light.
We can stop confusing God's patience with permission.
We can stop believing that our reputation is more precious than our relationship with Him.
And we can come to Jesus Christ, who gave Himself for sinners and rose again so that those who trust in Him may receive forgiveness and new life.
The Gospel is not the announcement that we have done no wrong.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ has done what we could never do to save us from our sin.
And that changes everything.
Maybe you have been pretending for years.
Maybe the smile has become exhausting.
Maybe the excuses no longer comfort you.
Maybe there is a confession you have been postponing because you are afraid of what truth will cost.
Do not confuse coming into the light with the end of hope.
For the repentant sinner, it can be the beginning of a life no longer ruled by hiding.
Jesus said in John 8:36:
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.” (KJV)
Not freedom to continue destroying ourselves while calling it righteousness.
Freedom from sin's dominion.
Freedom to walk in truth.
Freedom to learn obedience.
Freedom to live as people who have been shown mercy.
And if you have already repented and trusted Christ, do not keep treating forgiven sin as though His sacrifice were insufficient.
Receive His forgiveness with humility.
Make appropriate amends where possible.
Continue walking in the light.
And remember that sanctification is a lifelong work of God's grace.
The same Jesus who calls you to repent is the Jesus who receives sinners who come to Him.
So tonight, or whenever these words find you, ask yourself one final question.
Am I more concerned with appearing innocent before people than being honest before God?
Do not rush past that question.
Let it search you.
Let Scripture correct you.
Let the mercy of Christ draw you nearer.
And if you want to respond publicly, perhaps the simplest words are enough:
“Lord Jesus, teach me to walk in truth.”
There is no need to confess intimate details in a comment section. Bring your sins to God, and seek trusted pastoral or professional support where appropriate.
Because the greatest tragedy is not that a sinner has a past.
It is that a sinner might spend an entire lifetime refusing the mercy that could transform their future.

The heart that keeps saying “I have done no wrong” will never seek the forgiveness it desperately needs—but the heart that turns to Jesus will find that grace is greater than the sin it finally dares to confess.
